[[File:Ulota crispa (30083650062).jpg|alt=|thumb|''U. crispa'' growing as an epiphyte on a tree]]
'''''Ulota''''' is a [[genus]] of [[moss]]es comprising 69 [[species]] with a worldwide distribution, though most species are found in the [[Southern Hemisphere|southern hemisphere]].

They have commonly been grouped within the genus ''[[Orthotrichum]]'', though recently they have been placed in their own genus. Their phylogeny and taxonomy have been an area of debate ever since they were placed in their own genus, though it has been largely accepted to place ''Ulota'' as a genus of their own. They can be found growing on trees close to the coast, though some species are also found on rocks. Their shoots form small tufts to large mats across habitats, often intertwined with other mosses, including ''Orthotrichum'' species.

''Ulota'' reproduce using sexual structures, [[sporangium]] (''plural:'' sporangia), that are terminal on the shoot. The [[calyptra]] covering the developing sporangium can be hairy or not hairy depending on the species, but the hairs extend from the sporangium base to the apex as opposed to the calyptra hairs of ''[[Polytrichum]]'' mosses which extend from the apex to the base.

==Taxonomy==
Due to morphological similarities, this genus has often been taxonomically clustered with the genus ''[[Orthotrichum]]'', and has also been considered as a [[subgenus]] of ''Orthotrichum''.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Mitten|first=William|url=https://play.google.com/store/books/details?id=0yhHAQAAMAAJ&rdid=book-0yhHAQAAMAAJ&rdot=1|title=Musci Austro-Americani: Sive Enumeratio Muscorum Omnium Austro-Americanorum Mihi Hucusque Cognitorum, Eorum Praecipue in Terris Amazonicis Andinisque Ricardo Spruceo Lectorum|date=1869|publisher=Longmans, Green, Reader, & Dyer|language=en}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Garilleti|first1=Ricardo|last2=Mazimpaka|first2=Vicente|last3=Lara|first3=Francisco|date=2015|title=Ulota larrainii (Orthotrichoideae, Orthotrichaceae, Bryophyta) a new species from Chile, with comments on the worldwide diversification of the genus|url=https://www.biotaxa.org/Phytotaxa/article/view/phytotaxa.217.2.3|journal=Phytotaxa|volume=217|issue=2|pages=133–144|doi=10.11646/phytotaxa.217.2.3|via=Biotaxa|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Often, these two genus are found growing together. Mohr first segregated ''Ulota'' from ''Orthotrichum'' in 1806, though the segregation has been debated. The two distinguishing features were the splitting of the calyptra at the base and the curled edges of the leaves. However, some ''Orthotrichum'' species also have calyptrae which split at the base.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=Wang|first1=Qing-Hua|last2=Jia|first2=Yu|date=November 2012|title=A taxonomic revision of the Asian species of Ulota Mohr (Orthotrichaceae)|journal=The Bryologist|volume=115|issue=3|pages=412–443|doi=10.1639/0007-2745-115.3.412|s2cid=86387122|issn=0007-2745}}</ref> Molecular data has made some progress as to differentiating the taxa, though certain morphological features can be distinguishing.<ref name=":3" /> ''Ulota'' have superficial [[stoma]]ta, whereas ''Orthotrichum'' have cryptoporous stomata.  Other distinguishing features of ''Ulota'' include being [[monoicous]], and the absence of [[Asexual reproduction|asexual]] reproductive structures.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=Plášek|first1=Vítězslav|last2=Sawicki|first2=Jakub|last3=Ochyra|first3=Ryszard|author3-link=Ryszard Ochyra|last4=Szczecińska|first4=Monika|last5=Kulik|first5=Tomasz|date=2015|title=New taxonomical arrangement of the traditionally conceived genera Orthotrichum and Ulota (Orthotrichaceae, Bryophyta)|journal=Acta Musei Silesiae, Scientiae Naturales|volume=64|issue=2|pages=169–174|doi=10.1515/cszma-2015-0024|issn=2336-3207|doi-access=free}}</ref>  There is one [[dioicous]] species ''U. phyllantha'', and according to molecular studies it is closer related to other ''Ulota'' species than ''Orthotrichum'' species which can be dioicous.<ref name=":7" /> The hyaline cells at the base of the leaf margin also helps to distinguish between ''Orthotrichum'' and most ''Ulota'' species.<ref name=":2" />

Recent genetic analysis of the [[mitochondrial genome]]s of species within ''Orthotrichum'' suggests the presence of seven genera within the taxon. The seven genera include: the genus ''Orthotrichum,'' which groups together the three previous subgenera ''Callistoma, Pulchella,'' and ''Orthotrichum'';<ref name=":11">{{Cite journal|last1=Sawicki|first1=Jakub|last2=Plášek|first2=Vítězslav|last3=Ochyra|first3=Ryszard|last4=Szczecińska|first4=Monika|last5=Ślipiko|first5=Monika|last6=Myszczyński|first6=Kamil|last7=Kulik|first7=Tomasz|date=2017-06-30|title=Mitogenomic analyses support the recent division of the genus Orthotrichum (Orthotrichaceae, Bryophyta)|journal=Scientific Reports|language=en|volume=7|issue=1|pages=4408|doi=10.1038/s41598-017-04833-z|doi-access=free|pmid=28667304|pmc=5493672|bibcode=2017NatSR...7.4408S|issn=2045-2322}}</ref> the genus ''Leratia'', comprising the previous subgenus ''Exiguifolium'';<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Goffinet|first1=B.|last2=Shaw|first2=A. J.|last3=Cox|first3=C. J.|last4=Wickett|first4=N. J.|last5=Boles|first5=S.|date=2004|title=Phylogenetic inferences in the Orthotrichoideae (Orthotrichaceae: Bryophyta) based on variation in four loci from all genomes|url=https://www.scholars.northwestern.edu/en/publications/phylogenetic-inferences-in-the-orthotrichoideae-orthotrichaceae-b|journal=Monographs in Systematic Botany from the Missouri Botanical Garden|language=en|volume=98|pages=270–289}}</ref> the genus ''Lewinskya'', which includes the two previous subgenera ''Phaneroporum'' and ''Gymnoporus'';<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lara|first1=Francisco|last2=Garilleti|first2=Ricardo|last3=Goffinet|first3=Bernard|last4=Draper|first4=Isabel|last5=Medina|first5=Rafael|last6=Vigalondo|first6=Beatriz|last7=Mazimpaka|first7=Vicente|date=2016|title=Lewinskya, a New Genus to Accommodate the Phaneroporous and Monoicous Taxa of Orthotrichum (Bryophyta, Orthotrichaceae)|journal=Cryptogamie, Bryologie|volume=37|issue=4|pages=361–382|doi=10.7872/cryb/v37.iss4.2016.361|s2cid=88561982|issn=1290-0796}}</ref> the genus ''Pulvigera'', comprising only one species, ''[[Orthotrichum lyellii|Orthotrichum lyelli]]'';<ref name=":1" /> the genus ''Nyholmiella'', composed of the previous subgenus ''Orthophyllum'';<ref name=":7" /> the genus ''Plenogemma'', composed of the single species ''U. phyllantha'';<ref name=":1" /> and the genus ''Ulota'', comprising all previous species classified as ''Ulota''.<ref name=":11" />

===Species list===
There are currently 69 recognized species of Ulota, over half of which occur only in the southern hemisphere. This number also includes Ulota phyllantha which has been proposed to reside within its own genus.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" />

==Description==
[[File:Ulota bruchii (f, 144651-474826) 8609.JPG|thumb|Light microscopy of a leaf of ''U. bruchii'' showing the rectangular hyaline cells along the margin of the leaf.]]
[[File:Ulota crispa (b, 144647-474823) 0442.JPG|thumb|A mature sporangium of ''U. crispa'' showing the ribs along the sporangium wall.]]
''Ulota'' mosses tend to grow in a tuft on the substrate, with the shoots growing in an [[acrocarpous]] fashion with the shoots standing up.<ref name=":10">{{Cite journal|last1=Caparrós|first1=Rut|last2=Lara|first2=Francisco|last3=Long|first3=David G.|last4=Mazimpaka|first4=Vicente|last5=Garilleti|first5=Ricardo|date=2011-09-01|title=Two new species of Ulota (Orthotrichaceae, Bryopsida) with multicellular spores, from the Hengduan Mountains, Southwestern China|journal=Journal of Bryology|volume=33|issue=3|pages=210–220|doi=10.1179/1743282011Y.0000000008|s2cid=84279281|issn=0373-6687}}</ref> The tufts can vary in colour, ranging from a deep green at the top of the tuft to a darker brown/red at the base of the cushion.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last1=Caparrós|first1=Rut|last2=Lara|first2=Francisco|last3=Draper|first3=Isabel|last4=Mazimpaka|first4=Vicente|last5=Garilleti|first5=Ricardo|date=2016-04-01|title=Integrative taxonomy sheds light on an old problem: the Ulota crispa complex (Orthotrichaceae, Musci)|journal=Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society|language=en|volume=180|issue=4|pages=427–451|doi=10.1111/boj.12397|issn=0024-4074|doi-access=free}}</ref> The oblong to linear-[[lanceolate]] [[Leaf|leaves]] are attached to an erect stem, and can be slightly flexed to fully curled when dry.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last1=Wang|first1=Qinghua|last2=Jia|first2=Yu|date=2016-04-01|title=A taxonomic revision of Ulota Mohr (Orthotrichaceae) in South and Central America|url= |journal=Plant Diversity|language=en|volume=38|issue=2|pages=65–88|doi=10.1016/j.pld.2016.03.003|pmid=30159451|pmc=6112220|issn=2468-2659}}</ref><ref name=":1" /> The genus is characterized by the slightly to fully curled leaves when dry. The leaves have a costa, or midrib, which runs the entire length of the leaf.<ref name=":1" /> The leaves have hyaline [[Cell (biology)|cells]] at the basal margins of the leaves, which are typically [[square]] or [[Rectangle|rectangular]] shaped.<ref name=":4" /> The leaf base can be expanded or gradually tapered as it connects to the stem.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal|last1=Blockeel|first1=Tom|last2=Bosanquet|first2=Sam|date=May 2017|title=The Ulota crispa group in Britain and Ireland, with notes on other species of the genus|url=https://rbg-web2.rbge.org.uk/bbs/Activities/field%20bryology/FB117/FB117_Ulota_Tom.pdf|journal=Field Bryology|volume=117|pages=8–19|via=British Bryological Society}}</ref> At the tip of the leaves, there are cells with very thick cell walls.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Vitt|first1=Dale|last2=Koponen|first2=Timo|last3=Norris|first3=Daniel|date=1993|title=Bryophyte flora of the Huon Peninsula, Papua New Guinea. LIII.|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/272352200|journal=Acta Botanica Fennica|volume=148|pages=5–25|via=ResearchGate}}</ref> At maturity, the sporangia can be ribbed or unribbed.<ref name=":3" /> The sporangia sit on top of a seta, which holds it above the gametophyte. Between species of ''Ulota'', there is variation in the length of the seta which can be a useful trait in classifying species.<ref name=":5" /> The sporangia have [[peristome]] teeth are diplolepidous, with 8 to 16 exostome teeth and 8 endostome teeth.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":1" /> The sporangia sit on top of a [[seta]] which attaches to the [[gametophyte]] at the apex of the shoot.<ref name=":2" /> The calyptra covers the developing sporangium and is typically conic, split at the base, and can be naked or hairy.<ref name=":1" /> The [[rhizoid]]s are placed at the base of them stem, occasionally appearing along the stem, and are smooth.<ref name=":3" />

==Habitat and distribution==
''Ulota'' species occur typically in [[Temperate climate|temperate]] climates, growing as an [[epiphyte]] on [[tree]] trunks. Some species have also been known to extend into the [[tropics]] and [[subarctic]] environments.<ref name=":4" /> Multiple species can grow together in a habitat, often intertwined with each other.<ref name=":8">{{Cite journal|last1=Garilleti|first1=Ricardo|last2=Mazimpaka|first2=Vicente|last3=Lara|first3=Francisco|date=December 2012|title=New Ulota species with multicellular spores from southern South America|journal=The Bryologist|volume=115|issue=4|pages=585–600|doi=10.1639/0007-2745-115.4.585|s2cid=86367474|issn=0007-2745}}</ref> The genus is typically found in temperate, humid, oceanic coasts, though some species are also found in montane environments in the tropics and subtropics.<ref name=":3" /> Their habitat is found to be heavily determined by the available substrate, but also on the dispersal ability of the species and the dispersal obstacles that are present.  The species which tend to be correlated with the presence of ''Ulota'' species include: ''[[Salix caprea]], [[Populus tremula]], [[Fraxinus excelsior]], [[Sorbus aucuparia]],'' and ''[[Acer pseudoplatanus]]''.<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal|last1=Heegaard|first1=Einar|last2=Hangelbroek|first2=Helen H.|date=1999|title=The Distribution of Ulota crispa at a Local Scale in Relation to Both Dispersal- and Habitat-Related Factors|journal=Lindbergia|volume=24|issue=2|pages=65–74|jstor=20150006|issn=0105-0761}}</ref> They can also be found growing on rocks, though this is reportedly less common.<ref name=":3" /> Two species, ''U. crispa'' and ''U. bruchii'', tend to be found together, though ''U. crispa'' tends to be more common along the coast.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Albertos|first1=B.|last2=Lara|first2=F.|last3=Garilleti|first3=R.|last4=Mazimpaka|first4=V.|date=2000|title=Distribution and abundance of corticolous species of the genus Ulota (Orthotrichaceae, Musci) in the NW Iberian Peninsula|journal=Nova Hedwigia|volume=70|issue=3–4|pages=461–470|doi=10.1127/nova.hedwigia/70/2000/461|hdl=11268/5759|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

Within their distribution, four areas have the highest rates of endemism for ''Ulota'' species: [[Papua New Guinea]] (75%), Subtropical China (77.8%), Southern Australasia (78.6%), and South America (81.8%). South America also has the highest richness of ''Ulota'' species with 22 recorded species. The next richest area is Australasia with 14 recognized species.<ref name=":0" />

==Lifecycle==
[[File:Lifecycle moss svg diagram.svg|thumb|Lifecycle of a typical moss. ''Ulota'' species follow this general lifecycle.]]
Like other bryophytes, show an [[alternation of generations]].<ref name=":9">{{Cite journal|last=McMillin|first=John|date=1966|title=A Laboratory Investigation of the Mosses|journal=The American Biology Teacher|volume=28|issue=10|pages=814–817|doi=10.2307/4441553|jstor=4441553|issn=0002-7685}}</ref> The vegetative gametophyte generation is [[haploid]], and is dominant for most of the life history.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=During|first=Heinjo J.|date=1979|title=Life Strategies of Bryophytes: A Preliminary Review|journal=Lindbergia|volume=5|issue=1|pages=2–18|jstor=20149317|issn=0105-0761}}</ref> Most plants are dioicous except for ''U. phyllantha'', which is monoicous.<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal|last1=Sawicki|first1=Jakub|last2=Plášek|first2=Vítězslav|last3=Szczecińska|first3=Monika|date=2010|title=Molecular studies resolve Nyholmiella (Orthotrichaceae) as a separate genus|journal=Journal of Systematics and Evolution|language=en|volume=48|issue=3|pages=183–194|doi=10.1111/j.1759-6831.2010.00076.x|s2cid=84318916|issn=1759-6831}}</ref> Asexual reproduction is uncommon, except in ''U. phyllantha'', in which asexual propagules can commonly be found at the leaf apex.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Seppelt|first=R. D.|date=1978-03-01|title=Studies on the bryoflora of Macquarie Island|journal=New Zealand Journal of Botany|volume=16|issue=1|pages=21–23|doi=10.1080/0028825X.1978.10429654|issn=0028-825X|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Sexual reproduction involves the transfer of sperm from the [[antheridium]] (''plural'': antheridia) via water. Drops of water carrying [[sperm]] allow for the [[Fertilisation|fertilization]] of the [[Egg cell|egg]] housed within the [[archegonium]] (''plural'': archegonia). The heads of the archegonia have a [[mucilage]] which attracts the sperm, and the degeneration of the neck canal allows for the passage of sperm to the egg, resulting in fertilization. The fertilized egg develops into a sporophyte, which is [[Ploidy|diploid]], and protected by a remnant of the archegonium now known as the calyptra. Inside the developing sporangium, haploid spores are generated via meiosis. The seta raises the sporangium into the air, and once the sporangium is mature, the [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]] falls off and the [[spore]]s are released into the wind. The peristome teeth are [[Hygroscopy|hygroscopic]] and move in relation to the moisture content of the air, which allows for spores to be released over a longer period of time.<ref name=":9" /> Once mature, the sporangia are typically 8-ribbed, though in some species the ribs are only clearly visible right at the base of the peristome mouth.<ref name=":3" />

Spores can be [[Unicellular organism|unicellular]], although there five known species in which [[Multicellular organism|multicellular]] spores have been identified. Endosporic germination is the process in which [[mitosis]] occurs within the [[sporeling]] before the spore is released, and once released, it is considered a multicellular spore.<ref name=":8" /> This kind of germination is known in all three lineages of bryophytes: [[liverworts]], [[hornwort]]s, and mosses.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Schuette|first1=Scott|last2=Renzaglia|first2=Karen S.|date=2010|title=Development of multicellular spores in the hornwort genus Dendroceros (Dendrocerotaceae, Anthocerotophyta) and the occurrence of endospory in Bryophytes|journal=Nova Hedwigia|volume=91|issue=3|pages=301–316|doi=10.1127/0029-5035/2010/0091-0301}}</ref> Once the spores have landed on suitable substrata, [[protonema]]tal threads will begin to grow, followed by rhizoids which will help attach the developing plant to the substrate.  The leafy shoot develops soon after, reaching upwards towards light.<ref name=":8" />

==Conservation==
[[File:Ulota bruchii (c, 144704-474820) 5284.jpg|thumb|''U. bruchii'']]

Of the 69 recognized species, three of the species have been assessed by the [[International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.iucnredlist.org/en|title=The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species|website=IUCN Red List of Threatened Species|access-date=2020-04-05}}</ref> Native to northwestern [[Europe]] and [[Serbia]], ''U. calvescens'' shows an increasing population trend and is listed "least concerned". There is one protected area within its range, and it is listed as vulnerable in [[Portugal]], [[Spain]], and Serbia, and data deficient in [[Norway]].<ref name=":12">{{Cite web|url=https://www.iucnredlist.org/en|title=IUCN Red List of Threatened Species: Balding Pincushion|last=Consultant)|first=Nick Hodgetts (Europe LIFE project-Freelance|date=2017-05-20|website=IUCN Red List of Threatened Species|access-date=2020-04-05}}</ref> ''U. bruchii'' is found throughout northern and western Europe, with a few pockets in eastern Europe and is listed as "least concerned".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.iucnredlist.org/en|title=IUCN Red List of Threatened Species: Bruch's pincushion|last=Consultant)|first=Nick Hodgetts (Europe LIFE project-Freelance|date=2017-05-20|website=IUCN Red List of Threatened Species|access-date=2020-04-05}}</ref> ''U. macrospora'' exists in a small area within central Europe, and is listed as "endangered".  It has a small population size and the current threats it faces includes a decline in habitat area and lowering of habitat quality.<ref name=":13">{{Cite web|url=https://www.iucnredlist.org/en|title=IUCN Red List of Threatened Species: Ulota macrospora|last1=Vana|first1=Jiri|last2=Norbert Schnyder (University of Zürich|first2=Switzerland)|date=2017-01-04|website=IUCN Red List of Threatened Species|access-date=2020-04-05|last3=Consultant)|first3=Nick Hodgetts (Europe LIFE project-Freelance|last4=History)|first4=Irene Bisang (Swedish Museum of Natural|last5=Baudraz|first5=Maude|last6=Kučera|first6=Jan|last7=Ştefănuţ|first7=Sorin|last8=Lars Hedenäs (Natural History Museum|first8=Stockholm)|last9=Steffen Caspari (Zentrum für Biodokumentation|first9=Schiffweiler}}</ref>  Declines in air quality have also been correlated with declines in the size of the tufts of this genus found on trees in urban areas.<ref name=":14">{{Cite journal|last=Hallingbäck|first=Tomas|date=1992-01-01|title=The effect of air pollution on mosses in southern Sweden|journal=Biological Conservation|series=Endangered Bryophytes in Europe-Causes and Conservation|language=en|volume=59|issue=2|pages=163–170|doi=10.1016/0006-3207(92)90577-A|issn=0006-3207}}</ref>

==Uses==
''Ulota crispa'' and ''U. megalospora'' have both been found to be intolerant of high levels of [[sulfur dioxide]], which may indicate both species' use as an air quality indicator.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Ireland|first=Robert R.|date=2004|title=Review of Grimmias of the World|journal=The Bryologist|volume=107|issue=2|pages=274–276|doi=10.1639/0007-2745(2004)107[0275:R]2.0.CO;2|jstor=3244857|issn=0007-2745}}</ref><ref name=":14" />
